entries.title: Previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart shortlisted for Booker prize
entries.summary: The two authors are in the running for the £50,000 award alongside a Pulitzer winner, a science fiction legend, a comic writer and a debut novelist• Booker judge Mary Beard on this year’s shortlistThis year’s Booker prize shortlist features some very familiar names – previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are in the running once more, along with Pulitzer winner Elizabeth Strout and promi
entries.content:
This year’s Booker prize shortlist features some very familiar names – previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are in the running once more, along with Pulitzer winner Elizabeth Strout and prominent British speculative fiction writer M John Harrison.

Novelist and poet Luke Kennard and debut novelist Rebecca Perry are also in contention for the £50,000 prize, the winner of which will be announced on Monday 9 November.

James, the Jamaican writer who took home the prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, was shortlisted this time for The Disappearers. Set in Aids-era Jamaica, the novel centres around an attack on a group of queer men rehearsing John Herbert’s prison-set play Fortune and Men’s Eyes. Coming in at 640 pages, it’s the longest on the list.

Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain; this time, he’s nominated for John of John, which tells the story of John-Calum Macleod’s homecoming to the Outer Hebrides. The book is an “ardent exploration of the half-lives of queer men condemned to love, pine and suffer in silence”, wrote Yagnishsing Dawoor in a Guardian review.

Strout, who won the 2009 Pulitzer prize for her novel Olive Kitteridge, was previously longlisted for the Booker in 2016 for My Name is Lucy Barton, and shortlisted in 2022 for Oh William! This year, she is shortlisted for The Things We Never Say, which departs from the well-known cast of characters in her previous novels to introduce the history teacher Artie Dam, whose comfortable life on the Massachusetts coast is threatened by a secret, and by the realities of a changing US.

Harrison, who judged the prize in 2022, is shortlisted for The End of Everything, a post-apocalyptic novel set in an unnamed Kent coastal town. The book, “as its title suggests, is about everything”, wrote Michel Faber in the Guardian. “It burrows deep into our psyches – into the psyche of our civilisation – and exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now.”

The shortlisted books “took risks”, and they “could not be replicated by artificial intelligence – these are very human books”, said the writer Raymond Antrobus, who is on this year’s judging panel alongside the chair Mary Beard, Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, the writer Patricia Lockwood, and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu.

Kennard made the list for Black Bag, his comic campus novel about an actor in his late 30s who takes a job involving attending lectures in a black leather bag as part of a psychological experiment.

Completing the shortlist is Perry, the sole debut novelist, with May We Feed the King. The book – which won this year’s Waterstones debut prize – is about a modern-day curator tasked with dressing rooms in historic houses, who becomes increasingly obsessed with the life of a medieval king.

Four of the shortlisted titles are by men, and three of them – Black Bag, The Disappearers, and John of John – explore masculinity and male sexuality. That the shortlisted authors are predominantly male is “quite surprising, because generally speaking the male-written books weren’t as good as the ones written by women”, said Cocker. The masculinity theme may come down to men “having to rethink their role”, he added. Beard said she doesn’t think it’s a “very masculine” shortlist, while Lockwood half-joked that “all these books are gay”.

Among the surprises on the shortlist was the absence of American author Emma Cline, whose novel Switzy, which follows a man suffering from dementia travelling to a euthanasia clinic, received positive reviews across the board, amid predictions that it could win the overall award. British author Gwendoline Riley also failed to make the cut with her longlisted novel The Palm House.

The judges said the shortlisting meeting lasted approximately three hours. The five other books that didn’t make the shortlist were The Shadow of the Object by Chloe Aridjis, Helen of Nowhere by Makenna Goodman, The Renovation by Kenan Orhan, All Them Dogs by Djamel White, and The Vivisectors by Missouri Williams.

This year’s prize was open to books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.

Last year’s prize was awarded to David Szalay for his novel Flesh. Recent winners include Samantha Harvey for Orbital, Paul Lynch for Prophet Song, and Shehan Karunatilaka for The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.

entries.title: Britain’s Slave Traders by William A Pettigrew review – the inconvenient truth
entries.summary: This revelatory history shows just how deeply embedded slavery is in the foundations of modern BritainOne tedious aspect of Britain’s post-imperial melancholia is the number of amateur historians who would rather we stopped going on about our role in the slave trade. Isn’t it all in the past? Weren’t we the first to abolish it anyway? In April, the Reform party announced a new policy of halting vi
entries.content:
One tedious aspect of Britain’s post-imperial melancholia is the number of amateur historians who would rather we stopped going on about our role in the slave trade. Isn’t it all in the past? Weren’t we the first to abolish it anyway? In April, the Reform party announced a new policy of halting visas to people from countries seeking slavery reparations from Britain. “The United Kingdom is not an ATM for ethnic grievances from the past,” the party’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, said.

Unfortunately for those who would rather forget, the slave trade, as William Pettigrew argues in this grimly important book, can be found “in the depths of Britain’s grain”. Ninety per cent of the enslaved Africans transported to America went on British ships, and slave traders’ actions transformed Britain in ways that still resonate today.

The erasure of this history began with the abolitionists, who quickly realised that identifying and shaming slave traders might harm their cause. They chose instead to argue that abolition would confirm Britain’s superior moral righteousness. Lauding abolition obscured what Pettigrew calls “slave gain”: Britain’s gigantic profiting from the trade. Wilkie Collins and Charles Dickens, in a jointly authored article of 1857, blithely suggested that the gains of slavery had evaporated “as the Arabian Wizard’s money turned to leaves”. Thus began a general tendency to downplay Britain’s role, offshoring slavery’s causes and effects to the Americas or localising them to port cities such as Bristol and Liverpool.

Since April 2021, Pettigrew has led a group of nine academic historians identifying all the known investors – about 13,000 of them – who financed Britain’s brutal trafficking of 3.3 million enslaved Africans, of whom about half a million died during the Atlantic crossing. The traffic began in the 1560s with a syndicate of city merchants, naval and state officials. It soon earned royal approval, because of the role it played in humiliating the Spanish, increasing influence in the New World, establishing a foothold in west Africa, and enlarging the royal purse.

After the Glorious Revolution of 1688, English slave merchants loosened their ties with the monarchy and embraced a free market. The trade expanded beyond political and commercial elites, and out from London to the regions. Bristol and Liverpool shared out the trade in the 18th century, the latter perfecting and industrialising it.

In Pettigrew’s account, hardly an event in this period of British history – the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the rebuilding of London after the Great Fire of 1666, the 1707 Act of Union between England and Scotland – wasn’t impacted directly or indirectly by the slave trade. Slave gain funded the physical structures, from docks to canals, that helped make Britain a global force. The conventions of mercantile philanthropy also meant that it greatly improved the lives of the sick and poor, mainly through huge endowments to London’s hospitals. Institutions such as the British Museum and the Royal Academy of Music were founded with the help of slave traders’ donations. The Royal Society was not only a pioneer institutional investor in the slave trade but developed the racist “science” that perpetuated its inhuman practices.

Civilised Britons justified participating in the slave trade with what Pettigrew calls “an impressive degree of societal cognitive dissonance”. Daniel Defoe, an uncompromising satirist of his own society, promoted the slave trade in countless articles, arguing that it “exports nothing but what we want to part with, and it imports nothing but what we cannot be without”. Samuel Taylor Coleridge won the Browne Medal for classical poetry for a Greek composition condemning the slave trade; his education at Christ’s Hospital School and Jesus College, Cambridge had been funded by slave traders. Thomas Southerne, author of the successful play Oroonoko, with its unflinching account of the cruelties of slavery, invested £2,000 of the money it generated in slave stocks.

Pettigrew tells the story straight, with little reference to today’s culture wars. The most recent politician cited is Tony Blair. There is no mention of the opprobrium heaped on the National Trust for exploring its historic links to slavery; nor of the toppling of Edward Colston’s statue in Bristol in 2020, although Pettigrew does point out that he was a far less significant slave trader than other Bristolians.

But Pettigrew’s careful tone is ultimately more effective than stridency. In this argument, slave traders cannot be conveniently separated out; they become central to the British project of economic and technological progress and cultural enlightenment. The slave trade, for instance, was at the forefront of effective treatments for smallpox, the concern to save human cargoes from this deadly disease being a simple commercial imperative. Virtually any behaviour could be justified if it supported free trade, including the violent trafficking of children. “Those who fetishise economic advancement,” Pettigrew writes in a rare moment of acerbity, “must confront the role that self-interpreting economics has played in undermining African humanity.” Nigel Farage has said that he is “tired of this endless conversation about the UK’s complicity with slavery”. As this deeply researched and revelatory book demonstrates, the conversation has barely begun.

entries.title: The Complex by Karan Mahajan review – a superb family saga set in Delhi
entries.summary: At once a grand sweep through history and a domestic novel of petty differences, this tale of corruption and betrayal is packed with drama We learn about the murder of the Chopra clan’s shifty, crude, charismatic patriarch Laxman in the opening pages of The Complex. Twenty-five years have passed, but the stain on this once-respectable Punjabi family remains. The man who did it, Laxman’s nephew Bri
entries.content:
We learn about the murder of the Chopra clan’s shifty, crude, charismatic patriarch Laxman in the opening pages of The Complex. Twenty-five years have passed, but the stain on this once-respectable Punjabi family remains. The man who did it, Laxman’s nephew Brij, has served his jail time and is about to be released. Some relatives think Brij is too dangerous, too shameful to return to the family home, but his son Mohit decides the pair will live together – and rewinds the clock to tell the story of the decades leading up to the crime.

Karan Mahajan’s warmly received first two works, Family Planning and The Association of Small Bombs, explored individual lives alongside larger forces – urban development in the former, a car bomb’s traumatic aftermath in the latter. His excellent third novel has Delhi at its heart, but also visits Indian villages and cities, the American midwest and London, its short chapters flitting between different members of the Chopra family. You start by nodding in appreciation at Mahajan’s observant character portraits; before you know it you’re waist-deep in frustration, corruption and betrayal, as the book ranges through politics, faith, migration, infidelity and entrepreneurship.

The main stage for Mahajan’s epic yet grubby tale is the residential compound that gives the novel its name. This sun-eaten collection of flats and bungalows in the Delhi suburbs became the family’s base in the post-independence glory days of SP Chopra, a freedom fighter turned politician and businessman. Since his death from a boardroom heart attack, his nine children and their descendants have never quite lived up to his reputation, and the complex has become the increasingly ramshackle home of several couples and their offspring. Family members swap gossip, chide their servants and tussle for the best apartments, flouting building regulations and each other’s wishes as they go.

SP’s elder children are mostly distant figures, and instead we follow the youngest, Laxman, who half-heartedly runs a bobby pin factory and a local temple; Brij, a military pilot turned paper-mill manager; and Brij’s younger brother Sachin, who moves to Michigan to develop squeezable plastic sauce bottles. Around these would-be giants of industry, women find what power and release they can. Laxman’s wife Archana sneaks on to the complex roof for cigarettes and privacy, while Brij’s wife Karishma walks the weedy garden. In the US, Sachin and his wife, Gita, have both more space and more isolation, but the rest of the Chopras are never far away: on visits they demand tea at all hours and comment on the pair’s problems conceiving. The swaggering, entitled Laxman makes grim lunges at both Gita and Karishma.

As the 70s become the 80s, Sachin and Gita return to Delhi while Laxman, Karishma and Brij join forces to produce a line of ayurvedic balms. Children cram for exams and play cricket; adults bicker, hatch plans and do their best to ignore the increasingly blatant infidelity in their midst. Outside the complex, socialist governments become increasingly pro-business, Indira Gandhi is assassinated and Hindu nationalism rises. Laxman at first tries to mollify tensions, before becoming a vital player in a fledgling party that seeks to inflame them: the BJP.

This is a novel at a constant simmer, packed with characters who are all deeply flawed and often deeply awful. Everyone plays the game to one degree or other, confident problems can be solved by money, force of personality or the right favour from the right person. But the Chopras are fraying, and the Complex is at once a palace and prison, with its “glum black water tankies; the clotheslines savagely crossing the roofs; everything sloping toward death”.

Mahajan’s skill at getting into his characters’ heads means The Complex doesn’t feel as bleak as that image might suggest: it’s a wonderfully immersive and in-the-moment work. There’s beauty here, in marble temple floors “the colour of a thunderstorm”, or the image of Gita tightening her shawl to protect her “inky Banarasi silk sari from the cinders whizzing like miniature glowing kites” – as well as kindness, particularly in the sweet relationship between Gita and her nephews.

But the darkness is rendered just as vividly: cruel conversations around the snack table, vengeful nationalism, caste snobbery, the almost surreal horror of communal violence, Laxman’s grasping hands. This is a fine piece of work, at once a grand sweep through history and a domestic novel of petty squabbles. Mahajan drops enough breadcrumbs as he goes that the Chopras’ journey towards murder and radicalism feels less like a twist and more like a procession – but one packed with drama and life.

entries.title: Swan Song by Charles Spencer review – a furious exercise in score-settling by Diana’s brother
entries.summary: Amid genuinely touching passages about his sister, the earl can’t help but put himself and his grievances centre stageCharles Spencer’s Swan Song, a memoir of his relationship with his sister, the late Diana, Princess of Wales, is a fascinating document that tells us a little about Diana and a great deal about Charles Spencer – perhaps more than we needed to know. If that sounds snarky, after 400
entries.content:
Charles Spencer’s Swan Song, a memoir of his relationship with his sister, the late Diana, Princess of Wales, is a fascinating document that tells us a little about Diana and a great deal about Charles Spencer – perhaps more than we needed to know. If that sounds snarky, after 400 pages of score settling, chest thumping, wild indiscretion and some truly touching passages about his late sister, the reader is left with a head-spinning story of the world that created Diana and a certain sourness at the manner in which it is told.

Let’s start with the headlines in last week’s Daily Mail, the newspaper to whom Spencer sold serialisation of a book which includes a line describing tabloid journalists as “those who inhabit the murky swamps of malevolence, and who need to suck their victims dry of their souls”. Perhaps he meant a different set of hacks. Anyway the top line in the Mail was that, shortly after Diana’s death, King Charles insulted her in a phone call to Spencer: “‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough.’” Your take on this quote will likely dictate how you receive the book, and here’s mine: I’m willing to believe the king behaved badly, but “hissed” is a red flag, one of those embellishments, like “snarled” or “flounced”, that writers tend to use to make those they’re writing about appear worse. Spencer, always the injured party, has so many axes grinding away in this book that at times it’s impossible to hear what he’s saying.

Before we get to that, the question on everyone’s lips is: why write this book now? Spencer maintains it’s because, as the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death drew near, he kept being asked to contribute to other people’s projects. Rather than allow the narrative to be guided by “some TV producer” from a network “I will never watch” he promptly got on with his own. Likely that’s not the sole reason; elsewhere in the book he writes about how, back in the day, his father was always at risk of running out of cash to run Althorp, the family’s Northamptonshire estate, and one wonders if the present earl is having similar difficulties.

Never mind. For fans of petty grievances, among whom I count myself, the book is an absolute corker of resentment, and in Spencer we have a hero who, decades after the fact, is still harping on about a great many things involving a large cast of characters who he has absolutely not forgiven for any of it. While telling the story of his and Diana’s relationship, there are drive-bys on Peter Carter-Ruck, Princess Michael of Kent, Princess Margaret, his three ex-wives, whom he describes in an amazing parenthetical take down as “all double divorcees”, and members of a police protection squad who, in 1986, let sniffer dogs jump all over his furniture.

If too many words are spent on, for example, the perfidiousness of Martin Bashir, I could read an entire book on the subject of Spencer’s horror at what his stepmother, Raine, did to the interiors at Althorp, including installing “exceptionally ugly double glazing”, “shiny velveteen” upholstery, and “unsightly wall-to-wall carpeting”. (This is before we get to the scene in which Raine, standing at the top of the staircase in search of breakfast, bellows to staff below, “where’s my fucking egg?”)

Interspersed with these delights is a portrait of Diana that is affectionate, sad, and lovely in places. Spencer suffers the pain of the less famous sibling who doesn’t want to give up his own version of their childhood and there’s a stiffness to some passages as Spencer insists it was all less unhappy than the record implies. His portrait of their mother, Frances, feels like a useful corrective to a figure who has been publicly maligned, and who comes across in the book as the parent most responsible for Diana’s gifts: spirited, mildly eccentric, a more interesting character than the plodding males in the Spencer line. (Charles, winningly, allows that this is the case, pointing out that the men in his family have always been outclassed by the women.)

And of course there is the devastating account of the coldness and aggression of the then Prince of Wales. Spencer tells us that Charles’s poor behaviour towards his sister began from the very start of their courtship, during which he commented on her weight, ignored her at parties and told her he didn’t love her, to the extent that, Spencer writes, Diana tried to get out of the engagement. Their father told her it was too late. This all chimes with other accounts of the doomed marriage, albeit in gorier detail, and explains the fury of Spencer’s finest hour, the speech he gave at Diana’s funeral in which he lambasted not only the press but the royals, reclaiming the young princes William and Harry for their mother’s “blood family”.

At his best, in these passages, Spencer acts as a proxy for the rest of us by registering the absolute lunacy of those days after Diana’s death – by which I mean not the public outpouring, but the behaviour of the royal family, who remained deaf to the nation’s needs until they were forced to change course.

“What was Prince Charles actually doing there?” writes Spencer, incredulously, in relation to his former brother-in-law’s prominent role at the funeral, pointing out to some comic effect that no one wants their “ex” at their funeral? Diana’s former husband was there because the young princes were there, walking for two miles behind their mother’s coffin while mourners wailed and shouted out at them, an outcome Spencer had vigorously argued against. Now, he writes flatly, “It all seemed mad to me – the more so as I began to appreciate the extent of the ordeal we had embarked on.”

To be honest, at times in this book, they all seem quite mad. “That’s it ... it’s curtains ... Duch is dead,” Spencer reports his sister Jane as saying to him on the phone when news of Diana’s death was confirmed. Before the funeral, per Spencer’s account, Prince Charles wanted to walk behind the coffin in the middle, centre stage, until brought up short by his father, Prince Philip, who said words to the effect of don’t be so bloody silly, and put Charles Spencer in the centre, with the boys either side and Diana’s ex-husband and ex-father in law on the outside. There was a split second, writes Spencer, when it seemed as if the pall-bearers might buckle under the weight of Diana’s reinforced, lead-lined coffin. All of this is fascinating and Spencer tells it well.

Still, the book suffers from problems of self pity and self regard (I won’t get into the passages about Spencer’s ADHD or the weasily justifications he gives for telling Diana, in her hour of need, that she couldn’t move into a property on the Althorp estate; the main house has 90 rooms). Every few chapters we return to the unfolding play-by-play of how he wrote his speech – the decision he made to substitute the word “power” for the word “strength”; how his oratory gathered, his greatness formed, and look, it was a fantastic speech, but at some point in the book you start to think, alright Alexander Hamilton, give it a rest. Before the funeral, Spencer visits Diana lying in her casket and reads out his speech to her, sensing that his dead sister is “applauding my words, with soft insistence”. Even here, Spencer manages to take centre stage.

After the book’s litany of bitter grievances I came away wondering whether Spencer has been in the ear of his nephew Prince Harry these last few years. Mostly, however, I felt sadness for the insurmountable difficulties his sister faced marrying into that family. The king is peevish all the way through and Spencer is peevish right back at him. You come away feeling the pair thoroughly deserved each other. And in the middle Diana, 30 years dead, frozen in time and – as she ever was – at the mercy of other people’s interpretations.

entries.title: Doom Painting by AK Blakemore review – a dazzling epic of the Peasants’ Revolt
entries.summary: This recklessly ambitious doorstopper follows the 16 days of England’s medieval uprising from a vast array of viewpoints, and in startlingly rich proseAK Blakemore’s third novel tells the story of the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, when commoners of all classes – not only peasants, but merchants, servants, smugglers, and some local lords and officials – rebelled at the imposition of a poll tax and ramp
entries.content:
AK Blakemore’s third novel tells the story of the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, when commoners of all classes – not only peasants, but merchants, servants, smugglers, and some local lords and officials – rebelled at the imposition of a poll tax and rampaged through southern England, burning records of debts, killing their oppressors and laying waste to their homes. The book closely follows the events of the rebellion’s 16 days, employing a vast array of points of view, including the young king Richard II, several of his courtiers, dozens of elements of the rebellious Commons, a porpoise and a runaway horse. The title suggests the novel’s portrayal of these events as an inevitable reckoning; a “doom painting” was a picture of the Last Judgment on the wall of a medieval church.

As a book of this scope must be, it’s a doorstopper. As any novel by Blakemore will be, it’s dazzlingly rich in lexical glamour, and this is likely to be any reader’s lasting impression of the book. Sometimes it feels as if the author is out to use every word in the English language in a startling, aestheticised, puckish way that expands both the word and the world. The result can be joyously silly. Who else would give us slugs that “blurb their elementary forms from out of the undergrowth to begin a dank and toothless festa”, or “lunar-brilliantined mud”? But there is also gravity and passion here, especially when she intimately imagines the lives of the commoners: “they rise, to fry eggs in butter and pork fat; they rise, to whet knives on scarred stone; they rise, to braid the manes of their draught horses; they rise, to count arrows; they rise, setting aside their glitchy dreams of hairy stars and blue-skinned devils; they rise, fearful and powerful, into the bright day.” The cheekily anachronistic appearance of “glitchy” in this medieval scene is typical of Blakemore’s method. All forms of language, high and low, archaic and modern, are here. Her use of detail to convey a historical scene is also extraordinary: the barber’s chair where “a crowd has gathered beneath the ribboned pole to watch the draining of a cyst”; the brewer with “a grotty beard, chlorotic with hops, [that] hangs down almost to his belt”; or “the horseflies waltzing over the liquefying flesh of severed heads”.

Blakemore is less successful in the traditional novelistic areas of plot and character. The primary figure throughout is legendary rebel leader Wat Tyler. Historical accounts of Wat are few and unreliable, so a novelist has a lot of latitude. Blakemore makes him a mercenary traumatised and brutalised by the wars in France, and the details of this history fit well and feel appropriate. However, his actual personality fluctuates from scene to scene. Mostly he’s a coarse, unlettered bruiser, lovable for his simplicity. However, when he’s alone, he’s given to sensitive introspection, spending a lot of time assigning psychological explanations to his choices. In this mode, he’s completely apolitical, and his leadership feels like a tragicomic fluke. In other scenes, though, he expresses strong and coherent political convictions, and occasionally it seems his simplicity is only a mask he assumes to achieve his objectives. Other characters are similarly inconsistent or undefined, and while this doesn’t ruin the story, it does blunt its emotional force. We can’t feel that deeply about how Richard II was transformed by these events if he never came into focus for us in the first place.

Another problem is that much of the dialogue feels like action-movie banter in medieval clothing. People say things like: “Is that a scruple? And here, I thought you thoroughly divested of those,” or reply to, “I’d sooner die,” with a jaunty “You very well might”. The tone is occasionally anachronistic enough that it feels like a wink to the reader, as when Wat says, “We’ll sleep when we’re dead”, or turns to a confederate to say: “Your auld mum certainly seems to think so … Because I swived her, see.” Blakemore imagines a romance between Wat and another storied leader of the rebellion, Jack Straw; this could have gone to interesting places if it were made more real. But the execution is cursory enough that it carries a whiff of “shipping” – the demand of 21st-century fandoms to see the heroes kiss. Since the book is generally meticulously realistic and historically appropriate, I was left unsure how these elements were meant to land. In some places, the gorgeous language masks any clash of tones or realities; in others, the narrative fails to meld.

Despite these cavils, I very strongly recommend Doom Painting. If you have any sensitivity to language, you can romp around in its prose; if you have any political sensibility, the sweep of the revolt will draw you in. It recreates historical events extravagantly well and must have taken a colossal amount of research, yet it wears its scholarship lightly. It’s a beast and a challenge; in its quirkiness and intensity, it couldn’t be more interesting. In an era of safe bets and timid choices, here is a work of reckless ambition.

entries.title: Autumn by Kate Mosse review – tender reflections on time and place
entries.summary: The author of Labyrinth on the turning of the seasons and the lore and landscape of her beloved SussexKate Mosse’s new book is a love-song to West Sussex, part of a series designed to bring out its authors’ personal connections to a home landscape. It began last year, with Michael Morpurgo welcoming spring in Devon, where he has lived – at the farm that inspired War Horse – for over 50 years; and
entries.content:
Kate Mosse’s new book is a love-song to West Sussex, part of a series designed to bring out its authors’ personal connections to a home landscape. It began last year, with Michael Morpurgo welcoming spring in Devon, where he has lived – at the farm that inspired War Horse – for over 50 years; and then Val McDermid celebrating winter in Scotland, where she grew up and still lives. Bernardine Evaristo will explore summer soon – but, meanwhile, we have Mosse, also deeply and endearingly rooted in her chosen patch.

Mosse grew up in the village of Fishbourne. She now lives in Chichester, where she got to know her husband when they revised for A-levels in the shadow of the Bishop’s Palace, and held hands when she turned 17 on the day of the city’s annual Sloe Fair. Twenty-three years later, they celebrated her 40th there, with their children. Today, they live with his 90-something mother Granny Rosie – also “Sussex to her bones” – who remembers watching cattle herded in fields where a supermarket now stands.

In Granny Rosie’s youth, “the link between tradition and the natural world was present in every part of everyday life”, and that connection is the real focus of Mosse’s book. She has spent nearly all of her 65 years in Sussex. Her Languedoc trilogy was inspired by her time in the Aude city of Carcassonne, but it was Sussex that gave her a taste for the combination of landscape, history and storytelling that drives her books. The county’s folklore and countryside informed her gothic thriller The Taxidermist’s Daughter, and it was the backdrop for her memoir about family care-giving, An Extra Pair of Hands.

Autumn gives us more of it. Walking under oak trees, Mosse pictures far off days when oaks were the only road signs. In her garden, she tells us that the Romans called wild cyclamen “earth truffle”, “believing that ill spells were ineffective where they were found”. If there is, at times, a touch of the guide-book in her telling, she wins your heart by the sheer joy she takes in the details.

Mosse sets out what Sussex gave other writers, too. William Blake drafted Jerusalem in Felpham, then threw a drunk soldier out of his garden and was tried in Chichester for sedition (all because the soldier claimed he insulted the king). He was acquitted, but “never set foot in Sussex again”. John Keats was inspired by Chichester’s architecture to write The Eve of St Agnes; Hilaire Belloc became Sussex’s unofficial poet laureate; and James Joyce lived in Bognor Regis while writing Finnegans Wake.

Above all, there is “the great Sussex writer”, Rudyard Kipling. I love imagining how that phrase will be read in India; but, in fact, Kipling wrote Kim while living in Sussex (where he moved to in the late 1800s). Just So Stories came immediately after, and in 1906 he made the village of Burwash the setting for Puck of Pook’s Hill.

In the manner of Kipling, Mosse takes infectious delight in weaving her memories through bronze age camps, iron age forts, wetlands, the downs and the Devil’s Dyke, composing a hymn to Sussex’s countryside and braiding rambly byways of fact and legend with personal memories.

She loves the place so much that you feel she would have written as joyfully about it at any time of year. But she takes autumn seriously as a season of transition, beginning with her first day at school. There she is, 60 years ago, on 1 September: “Four, rising five.” Her mother is waving goodbye and her world is about to expand. Then, she takes us through the ghosts of Halloween, Bonfire Night in Lewes and Harvest festival.

By the time she gets to the last day of November, Autumn itself feels like a kind of harvest. Mosse sees it as a thank you for “the gift of home”. For the luxury of enjoying, intensely, the land where grandparents, children and grandchildren still gather; and for sun-dappled village Englishness. “I take a deep breath to try and capture my pleasure at simply being here.”

entries.title: The best books to read in September: new paperbacks from Margaret Atwood, Kiran Desai and Richard Holmes
entries.summary: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some great new paperbacks, from an epic multigenerational saga by a Booker winner to a biography of an iconic Victorian poet*** Continue reading...
entries.content:
Fiction

Fiction

The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny

Kiran Desai

This Booker-shortlisted novel is about work as much as it is about the relationship between Sunny Bhatia and Sonia Shah, whose families are neighbours and whose attempts to make a match begin their on-off liaison. Where Sunny dreams of journalistic success, Sonia’s heart and mind lie in writing fiction. The dilemma facing an Indian writer, she ponders, is one of obeisance to the west’s appetites and projections.

Desai’s solution to the problem in this immensely entertaining and generative novel is to dart continually between modes of representation and register. The gothic novel appears with the early introduction of the monstrous Ilan de Toorjen Foss, a narcissistic artist who seduces Sonia, suppresses her literary endeavours and then abandons her. The predicaments and predilections of Sunny and Sonia’s Allahabad relatives create a low-key bourgeois comedy: stranded single aunts, genteel impoverishment, the wrangle over a cook famed for his kebabs.

Capacious and shape-shifting though the novel is, filled with subtexts and shadow narratives, it is still a challenge to hold the contradictions and demands of multiple identities. Desai pictures Sonia and her father listening to the Pakistani singer Iqbal Bano, and reflecting on what the music conjures in them: “To be a citizen of a troubled postcolonial nation gave a person gravitas. To be holding out against the crass new world gave a man gravitas. To be wounded yet fighting on against the barbarians gave one gravitas. To be exiled, abandoned by love and luck, gave them gravitas. What happened within a family, what happened between a couple, was no different from that which happened in a nation under dictatorship, running on fear.”

Whether or not a novel can accurately and productively capture this yearning for gravitas, or the continuum between the personal and the political, is one of the questions posed by The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny. Another is the sheer exhaustion – mental, physical and artistic – caused by the constant need for self-invention and reinvention, whether individual, societal, national or global; and how the form of the novel, created in the European consciousness, can complexify itself to take account of an accelerated, fractured modernity. Desai’s answer to these questions is to make her story both dizzyingly vast and insistently miniature; to make us feel that there is as much at stake in the lives of Vini-Puri, a pair of servant girls not even accorded single-name recognition, as in the grand ambitions of the novel’s title characters. She pulls it off, not only in her manoeuvring of cast and incident, but in her ability to elicit apprehension, laughter, compassion and curiosity in the reader. Alex Clark

£11.04 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

We Love You, Bunny

Mona Awad

We Love You, Bunny, is the much-anticipated sequel to Mona Awad’s beloved campus horror/satire of 2019, Bunny. Both books are set at an Ivy League university in a crime-ridden New England town; from various well-seeded clues, we can identify this as Brown University. Here it is called Warren, because the Bunnyverse is unabashedly silly and self-referential. Rabbit jokes abound.

The first book followed Samantha, an alienated, cash-strapped creative writing student cold-shouldered by her workshop cohort, a cabal of four ultra-feminine rich girls who all call each other Bunny. The Bunnies wear fluffy dresses, eat mini food and – as Samantha learns when she’s finally inducted into their cult – express their creativity through demonic rites that involve exploding rabbits. Samantha has to transcend them to find her voice as an artist. The story of Bunny is the result.

We Love You, Bunny begins with Samantha bound and gagged in an attic. The Bunnies surround her, congratulating her venomously on the success of her book. Now they want to tell their story. Passing an axe like a talking stick, they introduce us to four versions of their Bunny-centric world. Then they pass the mic to a special guest.

This follow-up has the key strengths of the original, particularly its scabrous satire on upper-middle-class American femininity. However, it suffers from a certain sequelitis. It’s baggier than the original. Its metaphors for creativity feel less earned. The game of visiting each Bunny’s point of view also disappoints. This is redeemed, however, when we come to the last voice of the novel.

Toward the end, a writing professor passes judgment on the story we’re in: “A touch too camp. Zany. A sort of zany romantasy, isn’t it?” Yes, it is, but Awad is here to show us that romantasy can be serious literature, and nothing can really be too camp. And if We Love You, Bunny has weaknesses endemic to sequels, it also has their strengths. There’s the fun of meeting the old characters and seeing areas we wondered about before, but it also builds on the original, opening up new territory and making new jokes. And though it’s better to start with the first novel, We Love You, Bunny can be read alone. It’s a goofy, overblown flower of a book with lots of thorns that pleasurably scratch. Sandra Newman

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Buckeye

Patrick Ryan

Opening in the first decades of the 20th century, this luminous and tender novel follows the interwoven lives of two married couples in the fictional town of Bonhomie, Ohio. One half of the first of these couples is Cal Jenkins, the sweet-tempered son of a traumatised first world war veteran, born in the spring of 1920 with (to use the parlance of the era) a mild deformity: “The day you were born and one of your legs came up short,” his father, Everett, tells him, “right then I thought, well, that’s it. If we get into another big one, he’ll never be in it.” The delights of prolepsis!

The US gets into another big one in quite short order, of course. Cal, just as his father predicted, is turned away from the recruitment office and ends up spending his days in drudgery at the local concrete factory instead. A chance meeting with Becky Hanover, a young woman with a dark bob and a loveably whimsical way about her, sees Cal married by the end of the first chapter.

On 8 May 1945, Cal is working a shift at the hardware store owned by Becky’s father when a gorgeous, confused redhead stumbles in. Together, they listen to President Truman announce allied victory in Europe over the wireless – and then she kisses him. The gorgeous, confused redhead is Margaret Salt. Her own equally gorgeous and strangely aloof husband is away on a cargo ship in the Pacific. From here, the novel takes off at full thrust, and, as one of Ryan’s characters summarises it: “people get laid, babies get made, everybody lies to their kids”.

It is no surprise that Ryan cut his teeth writing short fiction: Buckeye is elevated throughout by the precision with which he captures the tiny, haunting glories of everyday suburban life. And for all its quotidian charm, a deep melancholy prevents Buckeye from ever tipping into saccharine nostalgia. Ryan strips away the Bakelite glaze of the American dream to expose the raw flesh beneath. AK Blakemore

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

The Wax Child

Olga Ravn

On 26 June 1621, in Copenhagen, a woman was beheaded – which was unusual, but only in the manner of her death. According to one historian, during the years 1617 to 1625, in Denmark a “witch” was burned every five days. The first time this happens in Danish author Olga Ravn’s fourth novel, the condemned woman is “tied to the ladder, and the ladder pushed into the bonfire”. Her daughter watches as she falls, her eye “so strangely orange from within. And then in the heat it explodes.”

The child is watched, in turn, by a wax doll who sees everything: everything in this scene, and everything everywhere, through all space and all the time since it was fashioned. On a basic level, the wax child is a useful narrative device. But it also complicates everything. The temptation, from the distance of the 21st century, is to assume charges against so-called witches to be baseless. But in this case, a well-known one in Denmark, the charges included the making of wax children – and Ravn begins with Christenze Krukow, a real Danish noblewoman who was accused of witchcraft three times during her lifetime, making this wax baby.

Ravn began as a poet, and even in English this lineage is clear. Her work asserts that knowledge inheres in objects, comprehension through smell and taste and blood and guts; through metaphor. “How do I know this?” demands the wax child, at one point. “It is like a gash in me to know it.”

At its best The Wax Child is richly evocative, beautiful, creepy and visceral. “It is the darkest of times, December. From the curvature of the earth, minutes run like droplets from the day.” At other times, there’s a bit too much research just out of sight; the novel can feel elliptical, even baffling. One misses the space, the clarity and freedom of Ravn’s International Booker-shortlisted novel The Employees. But maybe that’s the thing about weaving spells. About poetry, too: demand it makes neat sense, and you begin to have too much in common with the witch-hunters. Aida Edemariam

£8.49 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

King Sorrow

Joe Hill

Six oddball but doughty kids fall into the path of a vast and terrible supernatural evil which has come into our world from the outer limits of darkness. They must spend their lifetimes battling it, facing horror after horror in the process.

This is the plot, roughly, of Stephen King’s novel It (his best; no arguments). It is also the plot, roughly, of King’s son Joe Hill’s new horror doorstopper, in which six friends summon the ancient, infinitely malicious dragon King Sorrow from the Long Dark to help them defeat some baddies. Needless to say, their supernatural ritual backfires.

Joseph Hillström King started his career making great efforts to avoid any connection with his famous father, publishing under the pen name he still uses today and avoiding meeting his agent in person (he bears a striking resemblance to his dad). But in this latest novel, he leans into it. There are lines that deliberately echo some of King’s most famous (“The man in black fled across the desert …”); a moment that brings to mind a King plot point (a riddling contest). In this whopper of a novel, Hill is delighting in his family connection, and we delight along with him. King Sorrow is huge, sprawling – and absolutely fantastic. Alison Flood

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Memoir

Book of Lives

Margaret Atwood

Book of Lives is less a memoir than an autobiography, not a slice of life but the whole works, 85 years. Where most such backward looks are cosily triumphalist or anxiously self-justifying, hers is sharp, funny and engaging, a book you can warm to even if you’re not fully au fait (and few people are) with her astonishing output, which in the “also by” contents list here fills two pages.

At the co-ed high school Atwood opted for, she soon graduated to the “brain class”. A small, “flat-chested weirdo”, with horn-rimmed glasses, a snaggle tooth, frizzy hair, astigmatism and anaemia, she put her energies into sewing and fancy dress. By 14 she was dating: older, artsy boyfriends “somehow just appeared, like mushrooms after rain”. Poetry pursued her, too: her adolescent efforts were “heavily sensational, sometimes macabre”. According to her school yearbook, her “not-so-secret ambition is to write THE Canadian novel”. But her first publications were poems that appeared under the name ME Atwood, “so I wouldn’t be tagged as a girl”.

From university in Toronto, she moved on to Harvard, a tweedily unglamorous scholarship girl. There she researched the Salem witch trials, which along with the patriarchal norms of Harvard graduate school fed into The Handmaid’s Tale many years later. She wasn’t an active feminist in her 20s, when the idea that “domestic tasks might be shared equally” hadn’t arrived. But the oppression of women increasingly troubled her. And by the time the TV version was made, in the era of Trumpism, it was more salient than ever.

At a party in 1969 she met Graeme Gibson, novelist, trickster, spendthrift, high-energy oddball. He was wearing blue denims, she a “white crocheted lace mini dress with wooden buttons down” (Atwood is scrupulous in recording her changing outfits and hairstyles), and at first she had no awareness of his “non-platonic interest” in her. There were complications: she’d married an American poet, less from love than to spare him being drafted to Vietnam, and Graeme had a child by a woman with whom he had an open marriage, Shirley. A cautious courtship followed; Graeme wooed Atwood with yearning letters. If she’d not met him she’d still have been a great novelist, he said, but she’d have had a lot less fun.

His decline, dementia and death bring a sombre tone to the book’s last pages. Ever the workaholic Ms Fixit, Atwood keeps going rather than miss out on the publicity whirl for The Testaments (her sequel to The Handmaid’s Tale): “Ask yourself, Dear Reader: The busy schedule or the empty chair? I chose the busy schedule. The empty chair would be there when I got home.” She has a pacemaker these days and eventually her body “will decide to go off on an adventure of its own”. But for now mind and body are still together and so, in friendly opposition, are the many selves she unveils here in a “blizzard” of memories and photos: nerdy brainiac, waifish poet, Medusa-eyed feminist, uncanny prophet and one of the great novelists of our time. Blake Morrison

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

History

History

Indignity

Lea Ypi

It starts with a photo. A black-and-white image of a couple relaxing on a pair of sun loungers in front of a luxury ski hotel: him, squinting against the sun; her, smiling at the camera, wrapped in a white fur coat. It is their honeymoon in Cortina, up in the Italian Alps.

The year is 1941, and the woman is Lea Ypi’s grandmother. Ypi saw the picture after it had been posted online by a stranger, gone viral across Albania, and attracted a stream of abuse. “Morally degenerate” was one comment. “Fascist collaborator” another.

And so, in Indignity, Ypi sets off to find out exactly who her grandmother was. It is, she writes, partly out of a sense of duty, to defend her family member from the trolls – a kind of 21st-century version of EP Thompson’s famous call for history to rescue the dead from “the enormous condescension of posterity”. But partly, Ypi admits, it is because she finds the photo unsettling. How to reconcile her beloved, compassionate grandmother with this glamorous young woman living it up in Mussolini’s Italy?

From here, two parallel stories unfold. The core of Indignity is a richly reimagined retelling of Ypi’s grandmother’s life. Born in Salonica (now Thessaloniki) in 1918, Leman Leskoviku came into a world that was already falling apart. Cosmopolitan empires were collapsing into nation states, unsure how to treat families like hers: Albanian-speaking, living in Greece, with a proud record of service to the Ottoman state. Leman’s childhood is shaped by the uncertainty of those years: the trauma of wars just ended, economic decline, and blunt, brutal social engineering. As Ypi describes, millions were forcibly moved across newly drawn borders. Leman’s nanny, one of Salonica’s many Muslim Turks, is barely able to hold back tears as she is packed off to central Anatolia.

Amid the ambiguity, and to escape an unwanted suitor, Leman sets her own life on a different path. At just 18, she decides to move to Albania alone. Ypi’s Ondaatje prize-winning memoir, Free, was haunted by stories of Albanians fleeing to neighbouring countries to escape the violence of the 1990s. This story hinges on a young woman’s extraordinary choice to move the other way. Sami Kent

£11.04 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Politics

Politics

One Day, Everyone Will Have Always Been Against This

Omar El Akkad

Palestine has many eloquent defenders, and El Akkad is one of them. Born in Egypt, raised in Qatar and Canada, and now a US citizen, he has reported from the Middle East, Afghanistan and Guantánamo. His new book is a response to events in Gaza after 7 October 2023. It is his voice, his bafflement, spilling out after decades of having to keep quiet for the sake of journalistic neutrality or artistic show-don’t-tell, of having to bite his tongue after readers responded to his journalism with racist doubt: “I don’t trust any story about terrorism written by a guy named Omar”.

He turns his back on these old strictures and tells the world what’s wrong as himself, not just reporting but processing all that he has seen and heard. “This is an account of a fracture,” he writes, “a breaking away from the notion that the polite, western liberal ever stood for anything at all.” It is a deft, broken-hearted, rhetorical savaging of comfortable people who say nothing (or pay lip service) but care only about preserving normality, convincing themselves that these things only happen “to certain places, to certain people”.

One Day is passionate, poetic and sickening. It is full of well-earned rage, frustration with those who need this morality to be spelled out. For me it was cathartic, almost spiritual, to have these ugly truths articulated. It stoked and tempered the fires of my own rage. It is an important book, a must-read, if only for the reminder that history always comes down to one simple question: “When it mattered, who sided with justice and who sided with power?” Dina Nayeri

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Biography

Biography

The Boundless Deep

Richard Holmes

Alfred Tennyson was a divided soul. He even wrote a poem called The Two Voices in which dual versions of himself argued out the pros and cons of suicide. In this illuminating book, Richard Holmes has chosen to focus on the lesser known of the poet’s personae.

The Boundless Deep is not about the bestselling author of the nation’s favourite poem – The Charge of the Light Brigade – or the laureate lord, pacing along the clifftops of the Isle of Wight or posing for Julia Margaret Cameron’s famous photograph (known derisorily in his family as “the dirty monk”). Instead, Holmes gives us “young Tennyson”, the wildly talented youth whose story is far more rich and strange than that of the bearded celebrity.

The Tennysons, wrote Alfred, were a “black-blooded race”, meaning prone to moods and melancholy. His father, a reluctant clergyman, was angry and very often drunk. There was an incident, the details of which are obscure, that resulted in the family cook being burned to death in the rectory kitchen. One of Alfred’s brothers was confined to a lunatic asylum as a boy and stayed there for life. Another suffered from profound depression and followed his father into alcoholism. A third became addicted to opium. Alfred himself suffered from episodes of paralysing gloom and what he called “weird seizures”. His Maud is narrated by a madman: he must often have wondered whether he was or would become one himself.

Holmes is not an uncritical fan – he is tart about the pseudo-medieval flim-flam of Idylls of the King – but when he loves a poem, he writes about it with a wonderful capacity for noticing every pulse of metre, every flicker of nuance. This biography is a compelling story of an odd, brilliant, charismatic character, and a reappraisal of a man who had become so very established we could no longer see him. In giving us young Tennyson – gauche, beautiful, veiled in stinking tobacco smoke – Holmes has given the great poet back to us. Lucy Hughes-Hallett

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Biography

Crick

Matthew Cobb

Most people could tell you that Francis Crick, together with James Watson, discovered the double helix structure of DNA, and shaped our understanding of how genes work. Fewer know that Crick also played a key role in modern neuroscience and inspired our continuing efforts to understand the biological basis of consciousness.

Crick once said the two questions that interested him most were “the borderline between the living and the non-living, and the workings of the brain”, questions that were usually discussed in religious or mystical terms but that he believed could be answered by science. In his new biography of the Nobel prize-winning scientist, Matthew Cobb, emeritus professor of zoology at the University of Manchester, does an admirable job of capturing the rare thinker who not only set himself such ambitious goals but made remarkable progress in achieving them, radically remaking two scientific disciplines in the process.

Far from being the stereotypical reclusive genius, labouring in isolation, Crick was loud-talking and charismatic, a philanderer, poetry lover and thrower of risque parties. Crick’s inspiration and breakthroughs came through intense encounters with others, and he was skilled at bringing researchers from different disciplines together to solve scientific puzzles.

In Cobb’s telling, Crick was bold and arrogant, with an uncanny ability to uncover connections and to identify new theoretical and experimental approaches, often challenging far more established experts. Lawrence Bragg, the head of the Cavendish lab, is said to have described him as “the sort of chap who was always doing someone else’s crossword”. This approach meant he often stepped on people’s toes and was occasionally wildly off mark.

Cobb sets himself an ambitious task in trying to do justice to both Crick’s prolific scientific career and his colourful personal life, and this biography is an impressive work of research and scholarship. It is intended to be accessible to the general reader, with the advice that those who are struggling with the science should “follow Crick’s advice to readers of his own books and skip the hard bits”. This general reader struggled often with the technical detail and vocabulary. Some difficulty may be inescapable simply because the science is complex. Nonetheless, it is a relief whenever Crick is quoted, describing his research in his own words, because he had a knack for translating hard science into lay terms. Sophie McBain

£12.74 (RRP £14.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Technology

Technology

If Anyone Builds it, Everyone Dies

Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares

What if I told you I could stop you worrying about climate change, and all you had to do was read one book? Great, you’d say, until I mentioned that the reason you’d stop worrying was because the book says our species only has a few years before it’s wiped out by superintelligent AI anyway.

We don’t know what form this extinction will take exactly – perhaps an energy-hungry AI will let the millions of fusion power stations it has built run hot, boiling the oceans. Maybe it will want to reconfigure the atoms in our bodies into something more useful. There are many possibilities, almost all of them bad, say Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares in If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, and who knows which will come true. But just as you can predict that an ice cube dropped into hot water will melt without knowing where any of its individual molecules will end up, you can be sure an AI that’s smarter than a human being will kill us all, somehow.

Yudkowsky and Soares present their case with such conviction that it’s easy to emerge from this book ready to cancel your pension contributions. The glimmer of hope they offer – and it’s low wattage – is that doom can be averted if the entire world agrees to shut down advanced AI development as soon as possible. Given the commercial and strategic incentives, and the current state of political leadership, this seems a little unlikely.

There are certainly moments in the book when the confidence with which an argument is presented outstrips its strength. And Yudkowsky and Soares exhibit more than a touch of confirmation bias. “History,” they write, “is full of … examples of catastrophic risk being minimised and ignored,” from leaded petrol to Chornobyl. But what about predictions of catastrophic risk being proved wrong? History is full of those, too, from Malthus’s population apocalypse to Y2K. Yudkowsky himself once claimed that nanotechnology would destroy humanity “no later than 2010”.

The problem is that you can be overconfident, inconsistent, a serial doom-monger, and still be right. It’s important to be aware of our own motivated reasoning when considering the arguments presented here; we have every incentive to disbelieve them. It still feels like everyone with an interest in the future has a duty to read what Yudkowsky and Soares have to say. David Shariatmadari

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Music

Music

Night People

Mark Ronson

Night People is intended as Ronson’s memoir but is as much an attempt to immortalise the people and scenes he came up in as it is a reflection on a childhood shaped by the late-night parties hosted by his parents – first in London, where a distant memory of Robin Williams tucking him in to bed with “Nanu nanu” floats through, then later in Manhattan, when his mother marries Mick Jones from Foreigner.

By his own, self-aware account, Ronson has led a gilded life. Elite schools (Collegiate, Vassar, NYU); sleepovers with Sean Lennon and a cast of New York’s nepo who’s who; hanging out with Michael Jackson; the abundant creative freedom gifted by the safety net of generational wealth. It would be enough to make many readers roll their eyes before turning a single page. Their loss.

Ronson’s talent as a writer enables him to render this privilege, the background glamour, his awkward stumbles as well as successes, with a kind of wry, soft self-deprecation that is genuinely endearing. It helps, of course, that he is a massive nerd. Ronson would rather spend paragraphs enthusing about the thickness of slipmats required for a specific DJ setup than he would recalling the wild-eyed buzz generated at an afterparty close to dawn. On balance, this is a good thing. There is more than enough bad writing on hedonism in the world. I’ll take the earnest, qualitative review of turntable cartridges.

The one-man hit factory, the force who famously drove Amy Winehouse to create her best work, the mega producer – none of that is here, of course. At the centre of this book is a Ronson much closer to the teenage crate-digger whose mum bought him his first Technics turntables and who blagged his way to the booth. It shouldn’t be as compelling as it is, but for the accompanying soundtrack of deep cuts alone, Night People is well worth a spin. Nosheen Iqbal
